text: One day a young Italian. <break time="0.8s" /> Who had been selling penny ices from a small green handcart. <break time="0.8s" /> Appeared at my door. <break time="0.8s" /> And though he spoke hardly a word of English. <break time="0.8s" /> I took him on as both servant and model. <break time="0.8s" /> His name was Oronte. <break time="0.8s" /> And before long this cheerful seller of ices. <break time="0.8s" /> Dressed in borrowed English clothes. <break time="0.8s" /> Was posing as the hero of Rutland Ramsay. <break time="0.8s" /> And looking every inch a gentleman. <break time="0.8s" /> The Major finding his place taken. <break time="0.8s" /> By a former street seller. <break time="0.8s" /> Asked me with forced lightness. <break time="0.8s" /> Whether this was my idea of an English gentleman. <break time="0.8s" /> And I could see. <break time="0.8s" /> How deeply the question hurt him. <break time="0.8s" /> To be placed below a servant and a cockney girl. <break time="0.8s" /> Was a humiliation. <break time="0.8s" /> That no one of their class could have imagined. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet they bore it in silence. <break time="0.8s" /> Still hoping that their turn would come. <break time="0.8s" /> Then my friend Jack Hawley. <break time="0.8s" /> A painter whose judgment I trusted. <break time="0.8s" /> Returned from abroad. <break time="0.8s" /> And, looking over the Rutland Ramsay drawings. <break time="0.8s" /> With a fresh eye. <break time="0.8s" /> He declared that the work was simply bad. <break time="0.8s" /> They will not do he said of the Monarchs. <break time="0.8s" /> Warning me in his blunt way. <break time="0.8s" /> That I must get back into my boat at once. <break time="0.8s" /> Or I would go straight to the bottom. <break time="0.8s" /> The warning was serious. <break time="0.8s" /> For the publishers had also begun to doubt my drawings. <break time="0.8s" /> And my share in the rest of the series. <break time="0.8s" /> Was to depend entirely on the satisfaction. <break time="0.8s" /> I should give with the first book. <break time="0.8s" /> I knew that Hawley was right. <break time="0.8s" /> And yet so much did I pity the Monarchs. <break time="0.8s" /> That, for a while longer, I kept them on giving them the minor parts. <break time="0.8s" /> And telling myself that they might still improve.
